name: ReMe

paper.title: Remember Me, Refine Me: A Dynamic Procedural Memory Framework for Experience-Driven Agent Evolution

construction.unit: experience: when-to-use scenario, content, keywords, confidence, tools used (+ freq and utility counters)
construction.kept_as: LLM-written keypoint-level advice extracted from trajectories
construction.processing: from 8 sampled runs per task keep the best and worst; the LLM extracts 1-3 experiences from successes, from failures and from comparing the two; an LLM judge validates (score >= 0.5); near-duplicates dropped
construction.writer: summarizer LLM = the executing Qwen3 model in the paper (qwen-max in the code quickstart)

organization.stores: one vector store per workspace (Elasticsearch in the paper)
organization.index: dense embedding of the when-to-use field only (text-embedding-v4, 1024-d)

management.operations: dynamic setting: add experiences only from solved tasks; on failure, reflect and retry with the lessons; count recalls (freq) and successful recalls (utility)
management.conflicts: new experiences with cosine > 0.5 to a stored one are discarded (code)
management.forgetting: delete when recalled at least 5 times and utility/freq < 0.5 (checked every 5 tasks in the code)

retrieval.selection: top-5; an LLM reranks them and an LLM rewrites them into one guidance text
retrieval.budget: K = 5 experiences, rewritten into one paragraph

use.context: the rewritten guidance appended under the task text ('Some Related Experience to help you to complete the task')
use.reasoning: tool-calling agent loop, up to 30 iterations; retrieval only once, at the start

classify.note: In the released pipeline recall and rerank both use k = 5, so the LLM reranker only reorders the set a top-5 rule already fixed; the rewrite then merges all five.

stages.ingestion: The agent is run N=8 times per training task (temperature 0.9); per task the highest- and lowest-reward trajectories are kept for summarization.
stages.construction: An LLM extracts keypoint-level experiences from successful runs, from failed runs and by comparing the higher- and lower-scoring run; each has a when-to-use scenario, content, keywords, confidence and tools used, and an LLM judge keeps those scoring at least 0.5.
stages.organization: Experiences sit in one flat vector store, keyed by the embedding of the when-to-use text.
stages.update: Near-duplicates (cosine > 0.5 in the code) are dropped. In the dynamic setting experiences are added only from solved tasks, a failed task triggers a retry with lessons from the failure, recall and success counters are updated, and experiences recalled at least 5 times with utility/freq below 0.5 are deleted.
stages.retrieval: At the start of a task its query is embedded and matched against when-to-use embeddings; the top 5 are reranked by an LLM and rewritten by an LLM into one task-specific guidance.
stages.answer: The guidance is appended to the task text and the agent solves the task with tool calls.

summary: Procedural memory of LLM-extracted keypoint experiences keyed by a written usage scenario, reused through retrieve-rerank-rewrite and kept small by success-only addition and deletion of often-recalled but rarely helpful entries.
notes: VENUE: Findings of ACL 2026, pages 16803-16822 (aclanthology 2026.findings-acl.829); arXiv comment 'ACL'26-Findings'. Paper read: arXiv v2 (15 Apr 2026). CODE: agentscope-ai/ReMe has been heavily reworked since (1,051 commits, package renamed); the pinned commit is the last one before arXiv v1 (2025-12-11), where the task-memory flows and the BFCL/AppWorld cookbooks live under reme_ai/ and cookbook/. RESULTS: metric 'other' with category avg@4 / pass@4 (success rates in %, mean of 3 runs); No Memory, A-Mem and LangMem are the authors' reruns (App. B.2).

sources.code_note: Last commit before arXiv v1 (2025-12-11, version 0.2.0.4). It holds the task-memory flow definitions (reme_ai/config/default.yaml) and the BFCL and AppWorld experiment drivers; the paper's exact run configurations (models, num_trials) are not published, so the cookbook defaults are read as the reference implementation.

headline: Only the LLM-written 'when to use' sentence is embedded; the question is matched against it, not against the advice itself.
The agent never sees stored experiences as such: an LLM rewrites the 5 retrieved ones into a single guidance paragraph under the task.
Most of the gain comes from updating the pool during evaluation: on AppWorld with Qwen3-8B the frozen pool gives 17.06 Avg@4 and the dynamic one 24.70 (Table 1).

paper_vs_code.paper: top-K recalled, then an LLM reranker refines the selection
paper_vs_code.code: recall top_k = 5 and rerank keeps top_k = 5, so reranking only reorders; the rewrite then merges all five
text-embedding-v4, 1024-d; in-memory or local vector store in the defaults and quickstart
quickstart launches the ReMe service with qwen-max-2025-01-25 for summarizing, reranking and rewriting

paper_vs_code.paper: lessons from a failure are stored if the retry succeeds; at most 3 reflections
paper_vs_code.code: lessons from the failed run are deleted from the pool and only shown to the next trial; if that trial succeeds, experiences summarized from the successful run are stored; the cookbook main runs 2 trials

open_questions: Does retrying failed tasks with reflections count toward Avg@4 and Pass@4? The dynamic setting both adds memory and allows retries, and the paper does not say how trials and retries relate.

The fixed-vs-dynamic gap mixes three things (adding memories from test tasks, retries, deletion); Table 3 separates them only on BFCL-V3 with Qwen3-8B, where the whole gap is small (44.50 to 45.17 Avg@4).
With an LLM rewrite in between, the ablations cannot tell whether gains come from the stored experiences or from the rewriting LLM adapting them.

discussion.takeaway: Procedural memory helps tool-using agents most when it is fine-grained and kept up to date while working: success-only addition, retries after failure and deletion of unhelpful entries lift Qwen3-8B above a memoryless Qwen3-14B.

claims.claim: ReMe beats No Memory, A-Mem and LangMem at every model size.
claims.evidence: Qwen3-8B average 34.94 Avg@4 / 55.03 Pass@4 vs 27.65 / 46.20 without memory; A-Mem and LangMem fall below no memory on AppWorld Avg@4 for Qwen3-8B and 14B. Table 1, §4.2

claims.claim: Memory can stand in for model scale.
claims.evidence: Qwen3-8B + ReMe (dynamic) Pass@4 55.03 vs Qwen3-14B without memory 54.65; Qwen3-14B + ReMe 44.66/63.71 vs Qwen3-32B without memory 40.89/61.52. Table 1

claims.claim: Selective addition, reflection and deletion each help.
The LLM-written usage scenario is the best retrieval key.
claims.evidence: 44.50 vs 44.00 (task query) on Qwen3-8B; the ranking varies by model. Table 9, Fig. 4
Qwen3-8B agent with Qwen3-32B summarizer: 47.83 vs 44.50 Avg@4. Table 5

limits: Experiences are retrieved once, at the start of each task; retrieval during the task is left for future work.
Validation relies on an LLM judge, which may miss finer aspects of experience quality.
Gains depend on the summarizer; better summarization with small models is open.
reading: Only the when-to-use sentence is embedded, so retrieval quality depends on how the LLM phrased that scenario, not on the advice text.

In the released pipeline recall and rerank both use k = 5; the LLM reranker reorders five items that are then all rewritten into one paragraph, so its effect on content is limited to emphasis (Table 4 still reports +1.7 Avg@4 for rerank alone).
Most of the benefit on AppWorld comes from the dynamic setting (Qwen3-8B 17.06 fixed vs 24.70 dynamic Avg@4), which learns from the test tasks themselves while evaluating and also allows retries.
Table 4 is run with thinking off (No Memory 24.41) while Table 1 uses thinking on for BFCL-V3 (No Memory 40.33), so its numbers are not comparable with the main table.
The paper names two embedders (text-embedding-v4 in §4.1, Qwen3-Embedding in App. B.4.2); the code defaults to text-embedding-v4.
A-Mem and LangMem were adapted to procedural memory with prompt changes by the authors; both fall below no memory on AppWorld Avg@4 for Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B.

abstract.text: ReMe is a procedural memory for tool-using LLM agents that treats the memory as something to refine, not only to accumulate. From past runs, an LLM distils short experiences about key steps: what made successes work, what triggered failures, and what separated better from worse attempts. For a new task, experiences whose usage scenario matches are retrieved, reranked and rewritten into guidance tailored to the task. While the agent works, only successful runs add experiences, failures prompt a reflective retry, and experiences that are often recalled but rarely help are deleted. On BFCL-V3 and AppWorld with Qwen3 models the authors report the best results among the memory systems they compare, with Qwen3-8B plus ReMe beating a memoryless Qwen3-14B.
